p: I think it is a fair conversation to have.

Alright, you walk that back a little bit. Alright, you're an attorney, Mr. Ochoa. No, I'm kidding. Alright, I'm going to pivot to rebasing, and then I'm going to let my— I have a bunch of questions, but I want to let my colleagues

ask more questions. On December 26, 2025, the Comptroller's Office released a report examining DDC's cost and timeline tracking, among other processes. It found that DDC often changes the starting and endpoint dates when calculating delays. The report states, “DDC does not track all delays from the beginning. It rebases the starting point for counting days to completion as projects progress, continually replacing the completion date before reporting outcomes. The reporting— the reported figures are therefore distorted and total changes in time are obscured.” Why does DDC rebase the starting point for counting days to completion as the project progresses?

You know, Council Member, it is my third day, so I haven't specifically asked that question, but I imagine it has to do with scope changes. If there's a significant scope change from the sponsor agency— and I believe this is to be true, but our folks at DDC can correct me if I'm wrong. If there's a significant scope change that does require us to go back to front-end planning, it would set up the clock because the project, it is essentially restarting. And so if that's the

situation, I would agree with– in pushing back to that statement, but I need to do a bit more research on that and talk to my team.
I mean, yeah. I mean, if you're a member of the public and you say the project will be done– XYZ project will be done by–
[interposing] Yeah, they don’t care about scope changes, right.
You know, they don't care. They don't— the scope change for them is the project is not being done by the deadline that was agreed to.
Yeah.

That's the confusion. So if DDC routinely changes the completion date before reporting outcomes, how does this affect reporting? And has DDC taken any steps to change this practice in order to get a more accurate understanding of the capital project delays? I have some constituents from my district who are actually in— probably in the overflow room right now. Hello, Anne. Hello, Jack. Nice to see you. You know, they're— you know, we've been told many a time. I mean, the rebases— the rebasing has happened there.

All of– these things are just real for folks, you know, deadlines and timelines. And it just does— that doesn't make sense that we are– we're not counting that as part of a delay.

Listen, I think it's a fair conversation to have. I don't think the public will care about scope changes or any other reasons for rebasing timelines. I think the timeline that we put up front should be as close to the timeline that we abide ourselves by. There are, as I mentioned, for street reconstruction projects, there's always something that we, you know, dig up where that we didn't expect. So it does produce longer timelines. But I think it's a fair conversation, it's a fair point, and I'm happy to talk to my team about it.
Chair, I'm going to have one more question. Actually, Chair Sanchez, you can go now. Sorry, Council Member Sanchez.
I'll take— Chair, no, I'm kidding.
You’re co-chair of this one. You can. We'll welcome you.
No, no. Thank you, Majority Leader, and thank you, Chairs. I– you know, why does child care end at 3:30? Yeah.
Mayor's working on it.
Yeah. I thought I wasn't going to get a chance, but I– thank you for— congratulations on your appointment.
Thank you, Council Member.
Very excited to work with you and solve some, you know, long-standing issues. I'm doing the thing where I highlight the local issues, so you know, thank you in advance.
Okay.

But it's two different issues, but connecting it to the bigger picture. So one, I have a nonprofit that DDC is helping with the roof reconstruction. It's been a long-standing discussion at Kingsbridge Heights Community Center, and right now their concern is having to cease operations during the roof reconstruction and meeting DOE requirements. So, the broad question is how does DDC take into account

these kind of impacts to the budget of a local organization or a cultural organization during the scoping planning process? First, and then second, I have, Davidson Community Center, who was promised a second floor during the 2018 Jerome Avenue rezoning. So eight years ago. And just a couple of weeks ago we got an email from folks at DDC saying that there was a need for a wall strength test for the second floor that was revealed a couple of weeks ago.
Sure.

That is the promise. That was the promise eight years ago, a second floor. How is this coming up now? So, you know, one is the, you know, taking into account programmatic impacts into the budgeting process for a project? And two is, you know, how is it possible that concerns like this can come up for what is a central question for a project?
Yeah. I will take the Davidson Avenue Community Center, and then, Jeff, feel free to tackle the first one.
Hi, Jeff.

This is– listen, it is frustrating for any organization, let alone a

small one, to have a project, you know, be eight years and not move forward. My understanding is that it's in preliminary design. We cannot build the second floor unless we know that the building can stand a second floor. But that conversation should have happened a while ago. So I— let me look into it, Council Member. I share— I understand your frustration, community's frustration. I think we need– the only thing I would ask of you is if we need to nudge the sponsor and the community organization to— and if you need to bring us a table, I will be there to make sure that we are engaging, because sometimes there's a game of broken telephone that can, you know, lead to months and months delays.
Thank you. You're signing up for a lot of meetings today.

Keeping us busy. Thank you, Council Members. So, the short answer is both these buildings are very old. I know we've talked about that. There are some unknowns here. Because of the way Davidson was funded, obviously, we want to expand that scope, but this was— we talk about front-end planning. Once you start adding scope, it does impact everything. So it

started as an elevator project, as you know, and now we're working to see if that second floor can be added, if the building, the wall can hold that weight. So we will have results for you very soon. I do think we want to sit down with you and Commissioner Ochoa to talk with the organization to make sure we're aligned and moving forward together.
Great. And then on the–

[interposing] Sure. So we did have the pleasure of meeting with the Executive Director of Kingsbridge along with our Deputy Mayor's Office. Her team was very involved as well. So, obviously anytime we have to relocate an organization, we recognize there's an impact. There are cost implications and time implications for phasing a project. So, I think right now we're trying to look at what the condition of— there's two roofs if I understand correctly, and right now we're starting the process of probing those roofs. We're also working around their schedule, so we're not impacting during those probes. Once we have those probes, we'll know exactly what we need to do to rehab both of those roofs, and then we can come

back and talk about that, the moving around, if that's a feasible solution.
And would the city be able to assist them with any cost additions?
So that was a conversation. It’s a Parks facility, as you know, so those conversations are ongoing, but we can circle back on that one as well.
Great, thank you. Thank you, chairs, for the time.

Thank you so much, Council Member Sanchez, for those great questions. You're good? Okay. Great. I just firstly want to thank you both for being here and for the thoughtfulness and the energy you bring to this work. And I'm really hopeful in this administration's commitment to delivering excellent government services that we're going to see real improvement. We Chair Williams and Abreu and I really wanted to hold this hearing because this is an area where we are simply not delivering excellent government services. And so you all have a lot of work to do to do better. And I’m impressed by both of the breadth of knowledge and thoughtfulness that you have brought to the

testimony and the questions today. But I think that what you, you know, would have heard from more council members is a sense of frustration. And I think for many of the cultural institutions, libraries, other city agencies, if they were allowed to testify and tell you their real opinions, would be a lot of frustration as well. Maybe you could put on your old DOT hat for a minute. The– I'm just kidding. So, you know, I'll just, like– I'll give examples of things that just piss me off. Like In 2019, the de Blasio administration funded a pedestrian expansion and safety project on Flatbush Avenue that was supposed to make it safer at seven intersections. I think the best-case scenario at this point is it's going to be completed in 2029. Probably it'll slip into term two of the next— of the Mayor. So that's four mayoral terms for us to complete a street safety project. You know, we've had– we have a courthouse in downtown Brooklyn at 360 Adams. You may have read in the newspaper today, we're– I'm trying desperately to evict the judges from their parking lot. But there's been scaffolding up at that courthouse for 20 freaking years, right? Like, there are kids who have graduated high school who are younger than the

scaffolding that's up at this courthouse. We finally got DDC to start work on that recently. But it's been enormously frustrating and it undermines quality of life, safety, etc. I could give you a list of 10 of these projects off the top of my head that I have, you know, screamed at, you know, tried to cajole, massage any way we can to move these projects forward. And it just feels like they're stuck. When I work with DOT, I try to do everything I can to avoid a capital project because I know that it's my successor's successor that's going to have the chance to celebrate its completion. It's just like, what's the damn point? I'd rather do everything I can be expense. When I work with the Department of Cultural Affairs for the smaller cultural institutions in my district, I just don't give them money anymore for capital projects because they're going to want to spend the next two years on the phone with me telling me why their project can't move forward. And it's just not worth my time or their time for nothing to move. And I'd rather put the money into something that can actually get done. So that's just the frustration that I bring to this. And I think my colleagues bring to this, and so I'd love to just get

some questions– I'll get some questions out, but I just wanted to vent for a second. This is not what my Chief of Staff told me to say today, though. She tries to get me to be the nice— to be a little nicer. So, Chair Abreu got at this a little bit, but I just wanted to dig in further on Comptroller DiNapoli's, recent report from last year highlighting the 5,000+ capital projects that 64 percent are delayed at least three months, 48 percent are delayed over three years. Do we have data on where we are today? Like, are you— could you— I realize it's day three, so I apologize if it's an impossible question, but like, could DDC answer the question maybe as a follow-up to us in writing of what percentage of capital projects that DDC is currently working on are more than three years delayed?
Yeah. I believe so, but it's the– what constitutes a delay question that I think it's— and I keep on mentioning because I think it's really important.
Yeah.

I think we would treat it as whenever we get the project and whenever we through front-end planning process we estimate a

timeline and then from there I would feel comfortable with— from there and without any major change in scopes I would feel comfortable having that data. I don't know if that's easily available in the way I think you wanted. I would give a shout out to the Mayor's Office of Operations. They have a capital dashboard that has essentially every single capital project in the city easily available for the public and the Council. I believe that data there is accurate.
Just to interrupt you on that for a second.
Sure.

My understanding of the capital projects dashboard is that it covers about 60 percent of the city's these capital commitments. So we do— we value it, but it is not comprehensive, and it should be. And so we know there's a new Mayor– I don't know if she's actually begun, but we have a new appointment for the Mayor's Office of Operations. Credit to the team. It came from a Local Law, just to note.
Yes.
You worked on it when you were at
I did.
So thank you for helping to get that through, and thank you to our predecessors in the Council for passing it. But I just want to note, we have work to do to actually make it comprehensive.
Fair, yeah.
I interrupted you though. If you were still going I can–

[interposing] No, I was just going to say, listen, I'm going to be looking at all IT systems at DDC to make sure that we have internal tracking, and if there's a way to put that externally for folks to have a bit more transparency, I'm happy to. I think I'm— again, there's so many legacy systems that have been, you know, that we've been using for a very long time that I'm very excited to look at how we can improve for the purposes of project delivery. But if it also helps for transparency, I'm open to that.

You know, it's– our goal on transparency is to bring accountability,

right? And so if we all collectively have the data and can look at it and can evaluate how we're doing, then we can push and say, hey, there's a problem here.
Yeah.

And if that data isn't clear, maybe it's clear to you all, but not to the rest of us, or maybe it's tracked in different places, like you were saying, the timeliness of a project versus the over budget of– the budget of the project are not necessarily being tracked in the same place, it does get complicated to be as tight as we need to be to manage things to successful outcomes. So that's the orientation here. We see phenomenal disparities in agency– in how sponsor agency projects are doing in terms of timeliness with DDC. Like, library projects are the most delayed. DOT projects are extremely delayed. Some agencies do better. I appreciate that, as you noted earlier, there's a wide variety of projects that you all work on. It's quite remarkable. But have you begun to think about why are some projects— why are some agencies doing better and some agencies quite simply not?

Yeah, I don't think it's a— it's an agency issue. It's more of a project issue. The higher the unknowns, the likelier the delays will have. And so, if a project is from a cultural institution of a building that was landmarked and built in 1895, you're probably going in through the scoping process with a lot of unknowns. And so– and same with street construction projects that, again, especially in Manhattan, there's a lot of work under our streets that we just don't know about. There's also subway interference, or— I'm sorry, I shouldn't call it interference. It's just subway infrastructure where we need GOs or temporary passes from the MTA for us to touch the— to even touch that infrastructure. So, there is a lot of coordination that needs to happen, but it's the unknowns that usually result in longer timelines. This is why, I mean, like, it's sometimes it's easier to build a brand new project, than it is to restore or renovate an existing one.
And I think you— I mean, some of the alternative delivery methods that you spoke to are easier to deploy on new projects.
Yeah, yeah.

Right? And as well. Back in 2021, some time ago, Center for Urban Future put out a report, and in it, DDC indicated that they were intending to shave an additional 30 months off their 96-month project timelines. My understanding is things have gotten down to about 90 months, so we've shaved some time off, but a long way off from that goal.
Sure.

96 months is eight years, 7.5 years. 66 months, still over five, not, you know, expeditious process. But could you help us understand— and I– in noting that, in the intervening years we had this Capital Project Reform Taskforce. You said some of those reforms are helpful.
Yeah.

We're still not seeing that make a demonstrable difference though. So what has been helpful? Can you quantify what reforms are helpful and what reforms maybe were proposed that haven't yet been fully realized that would be helpful for us to prioritize?

Yeah, so actually 2026 is going to be a very big year for DDC and

alternative delivery. A lot of the projects that we started under design-build, under the first design-build authorization are coming online now.
Great.

And those projects are being done in just a handful of years. I mentioned Shirley Chisholm Rec Center, which to me is incredible because I worked to fund it under the last year of Mayor de Blasio. And the fact that it got completed just earlier this year is incredible. That's the gold standard that we're striving for. But it is an alternative delivery project. And so design-build and expanding our design-build– I'm looking forward to all the briefings that I have from Jade and the team. But I think expanding the amount of alternative delivery usage throughout the agency, I think will really shave down those costs significantly.
So I did want to dig in on exactly that. So the city's authorized to use design-build specifically at about eight agencies, if I have this right?

That sounds right. I'm actually not aware of other agencies who want

design-build authority who don't have it. I think there was a resolution.

Fair, but the state has authorized us to do it with— through DDC, DOT, Parks, DEP, SCA, NYCHA, H+H, and DCAS. In your agency's report from last year on design-build, DDC noted that the agency had awarded 12 contracts valued at over $800 million. $140 million of it was for Shirley Chisholm, but, you know, you get a sense of scale. And the— it listed as of August 25, a total of 24 design-build contracts. What I– I think in— basically what I'm really trying to get at here is, should we be seeing more design-build contracts? Like, a couple dozen contracts across eight agencies over what's now been— it's 2026, so seven years since design-build authorization was originally granted. Like, shouldn't this be more— much more widely adopted?

Yeah, I understand where you're coming from. You know, design-build is sort of a new process for a lot of us. I think it also includes a lot of training for staff to make sure they understand all the rules of design-build, both on the admin side. So like the way that we

procure and put out a contract and the specs that a contract will have for design-build purposes, but also for the delivery. So I hear you and I understand where you're coming from, that there should be more design-build process, but it is a learning curve for our staff and for our sister agencies to learn about the expertise required for design-build. DDC has a close partnership with DBIA. The Design-Build Institute of America, that does a lot of these trainings. We've offered these trainings for our sister agencies. I encourage and I will be working to make sure that our sister agencies are taking us up on those trainings to ensure that there's— that their staff know how— what it entails to use an alternative delivery method like design-build. And with that, we expect more design-build projects to come online, too.

Okay. Could you— I don't— again, it's day three. We're grateful to have you here and be engaging. But if you could provide us with a comprehensive list of what projects DDC has engaged with design-build, it would be helpful.
Sure. Yeah. We can— we can— yeah.

Thank you very much. We will annoy you with follow-up questions in writing. I guess— I think you— you answered this for design-build, but just want to ask it a little more broadly. Are those the same barriers for why we're not seeing more progressive design-build and CM-build on more projects at agencies? Is it that same—

[interposing] I think so, though, although, progressive design-build and CM-Build, we got authorities after design-build, so I expect that same sort of learning curve to happen, but for CM-Build, we're definitely moving forward with the projects. My understanding is that for progressive design-build, there were some discrepancies in what we had asked for the authority, versus what we got. But I will be doing a deeper dive on all alternative delivery methods.
And do you feel confident at this point as we look ahead toward 2029 and reauthorization that we'll be able to make a strong case that this is really working and we're utilizing it at scale?

Yeah. Yeah, absolutely. And I think we have great examples. And

hopefully by 2029 we're going to have a brand new jail as well in Brooklyn to show for.

Okay. We're making good progress there. So, I wanted to ask a little bit about change orders and scopes. So, can you clarify the process for granting scope changes? Does any entity, kind of OMB, MOCS, contracting agencies, or like the sponsor agencies, flag vendors who submit high numbers of change orders? Are vendors' histories of change orders considered when awarding contracts? Like, who's providing that global analysis?

Yeah. It's a very good question. I don't have the answer with me. I– it is something that I know it's an issue. So I will see what data we have. I think it's a fair point to sort of flag if there's vendors who just, you know, utilize the change order process for, you know, nefarious reasons other than, you know, real change orders. But I'm happy to look into that. I think it's a fair point. I would say, though, we're— we are— we have done a lot of things to limit the change orders. And nobody likes them. And I know it was one of— one, one of the biggest points of contention or emphasis, I would say, in the Capital Reform Taskforce.

Is somebody from MOCS here? John Katsorhis, would you mind joining us for this? Thanks. Did we— do we need to do anything? We'll need a witness slip, but we'll do that after. Nice to see you. Thank you for being here today. MOCS's oversight on change orders— are you looking at— just the same question I asked the Commissioner. Like, are you looking at vendors that are submitting high numbers of change orders? Is that something that's being consider— is that easily available information for us to analyze through Passport?

So, first of all, good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for the opportunity to be here to talk to you. The– MOCS serves an oversight function of the procurement process, not necessarily digging into the level of detail about construction change orders and arriving at whether or not it's justified, we rely on the contracting agency to make that determination and review it. We know that there's a very thorough process to review that and determine whether or not there's relevance to that change order.

I guess what I'm asking is a little different, is a data question and

a Passport question, and maybe you may– your role is Deputy Chief Procurement Officer, is that right?
Yes.

So forgive me if there's a better person at MOCS to ask this question to. But shouldn't Passport allow us to kind of easily pull the data of where there are high numbers of change orders by vendor, looking at whether there are vendors that are abusing the process and kind of applying for the lowest bid and then insisting on change orders again and again and again and again that increase prices, and we had to go with the lowest bid, but then this shady vendor keeps adding change orders in that don't actually make it all that affordable, and we could have picked a much more impressive and reliable vendor for slightly more money that didn't apply for the lowest bid. Shouldn't Passport easily be able to identify that for us and provide that analysis for DDC and other sponsor agencies to be looking at so that we understand this information a little bit better?
Thank you for the clarification.
Sorry if I didn't— if I wasn't— if I wasn't explaining my point clearly or who I was trying to attack.

I appreciate the clarification. Passport does collect and capture certain information. We do include change order information in our annual indicators report that we have on our website. But I don't think it's to the level that you're describing. And so I would be happy to circle back with you on what improvements we can do to increase the transparency.

Yeah, I will just say I was hanging out with the DCAS Commissioner and Council Member Brewer recently, and they are getting new data from Passport on procurement spending that they've never gotten before that's providing, like, really helpful insights into the oversight that they should be providing on procurement decisions we're making citywide. And I think that there's a lot of information generally that we have in Passport that nobody's really been digging into and that DDC and others should be analyzing, and we need MOCS’ help on it. I think if we could make improvements to Passport, capitally eligible, it would be a lot

easier for us to see some of those improvements happen. So I hope that is something that we can all advocate for together with our friends at OMB and the Comptroller's Office. But that is a different– I'm now going on a tangent. Thank you for that. I appreciate it. Oh, could you please state your name for the record and you'll tell me if I need to do anything else? Okay. Great. The– our committee counsel would like to swear you in.
Sure. Do I start with announcing myself?

We'll have you raise your right hand and then you can say who you are so that it's on the record and we know that you're telling the truth. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?
I do.
Alright, thank you. Can you please state your name for the record?
John Katsorhis. I'm the Deputy City Chief Procurement Officer at the Mayor's Office of Contract Services.

Thank you again very much. We appreciate you being here. I am going to— I just would like to shift to project management a little bit at DDC. This was one of the issues that Comptroller Lander highlighted in his report as well. I'm trying to complement the things that Chair Abreu raised. He emphasized, and we've heard this informally from sponsor agencies as well, is that the unevenness in the skill set of DDC project managers has a big impact on project outcomes. And I was just wondering, as a new Commissioner, are you thinking about professional development opportunities for project managers, opportunities to measure accountability for project on— for the projects that they have in their portfolios around whose projects have consistent cost overruns, whose projects are delivered on time, whose are not? Is there— is there more that we should be looking at there, that kind of human role that you think could improve outcomes?

Yes, Chair, so I've had the pleasure of meeting a lot of DDC folks. I think I will say this is— they're incredibly dedicated individuals. They're all excited about the projects they're working on. I think what you raise

is an issue of providing them with the right tools to succeed. That includes both the right staffing levels, but also the right systems and tools. There's also— if there are lessons to be learned from very successful projects, what I'm— what I'm committing to you is that we're going to be sharing those lessons across divisions and across units to make sure that those– that what worked in one side of the public buildings, for example, can be shared across the different units and across that division. Same with the infrastructure team. So I think it's all about providing them the right resources to succeed. Both again in terms of technology, but also training and role models, if you will, across the agency.

Thank you. I appreciate that. For, the Associate Commissioner whose name I– let me— I don't have it. I'm sorry. Who's the— for the birthday boy. I wanted to ask about legislation that we recently passed for a DOT capital project tracker. Could you speak to the status of implementation?

Sure. Thank you for the question, Chair. So we have started looking at systems and models, how to build it. We're

going to work with our partners at DDC because they're integral to delivering on our projects, or a portion of our projects. We think that we'll absolutely be able to complete it by the timeline stated in the legislation, and we're actively going to work on it.
Since I'm not looking at— remind me of that deadline.
Let me get that.
Okay, thank you. And I'm sorry, Associate Commissioner Jaroslavsky [sp?]. I apologize. I hope I pronounced that okay.
Perfectly. it is in 2028.

2028. I wouldn't have been as nice if it was my bill. Okay, we look forward to having that. I wanted to ask a little bit about AIMS. I will try to not go on for too much longer because I know we have a lot of great people who want to testify. So, I'm very interested in how we are tracking the state of repair or disrepair of our capital infrastructure. Could you share if you're up to speed yet? I feel like all these questions are

slightly unfair, but does DDC do a state— kind of an analysis of the state of repair of city assets and a plan for routine maintenance?

You know, I was just talking to the Commissioner Katowsky [sp?] about this issue. I believe we have a meeting with NYCHA to see how they talk about the state of good repair for their assets. We— I believe we rely on our sister agencies or sponsor agencies who are the owners of the assets once we deliver the projects to do the AIMS report. As Executive Deputy Commissioner at DOT, I was the signatory for DOT. And so— but I don't know that DDC has the list of assets, because once we deliver, we sort of give it to either Parks or DOT or DCLA to manage. So I can get back to you on that. I do not believe, however, that DDC would manage the same—

[interposing] We had talked to Commissioner Foley about some stuff, some pretty innovative stuff that he was working on toward the end of his term, his tenure, that I think you'll really enjoy as well as you dig in.
Okay.

You know, basically my overarching critique is that I should be able to, as a Council Member, ascertain what's the condition of a piece of infrastructure in my district. Like, it's a playground, a bridge, whatever it may be, have pretty good detailed information that a city agency makes available to me for what's that state of disrepair. And then I want to understand what's getting funded in the capital plan for the things that are not in good repair. And we should have accountability on that. And if OMB is choosing not to fund those projects in the capital plan, they should have to to defend themselves. So we have some legislation toward that end. We hope to have a hearing on it in the near future, but I think DDC has a critical role to play, because I think you all have the engineering and architectural assistance and analytical ability to evaluate what is the state of good repair or not as much as any agency we have. And it's a cumbersome and big task, but I think it's really important. And—
Sure. We're happy to be involved.

Would love to discuss that with you further. The thing— well, we can— it's the advanced capital planning management system was the tracking of assets and planning projects together that I was really impressed by, and I think it's a cool thing that was— is— so, whatever. I will close by being a parochial council member, because that's my job. As you noted, Commissioner, the Brooklyn Borough-based jail is in our district. And it looks like you all have, you know, done a pretty good job of staying on budget on that one.
Yeah.
It's a big budget, but staying within it.
Yeah.
I understand that the Brooklyn contract includes a guaranteed maximum price.
That's how design-build projects usually—
[interposing] Every design-build.
That's right.
Okay. And So each of the borough-based jails have that, and that is an effective tool for us to stay within budget, essentially.
Yeah.
Can this be used in other contracts that are not design-build? Is that like a mechanism that we should be looking to expand if it keeps us within budget?
You know, we do early delivery incentives in a lot of projects.
How are those going?
Well–
Mostly parks.
Mostly parks. Let me get back to you.
Okay.
DOTs too. I think it's— it should be standard for— if not, I will make sure that it is a standard part of the contracts for our DDC projects.
Great.

But let me get back to you on whether or not the maximum price is

something that we can implement for non-design-build projects. I don't know the answer. I'll check with our legal.

I appreciate it. The– this is a plea that I'm making to many of your colleagues across the administration, but I'm going to make it to you today. I've made it to the Deputy Mayor and others as well. And I'm— multiple other commissioners. But my understanding is that there is some contingency in this contract that we've not yet had to use–
[interposing] That’s right.

because you've been doing such a great job of keeping us on budget. What I'm most concerned about in this facility is the lack of access to outdoor space. I do not believe that the outdoor space is currently designed within the housing units is outdoor space at all. And it may meet SEOC requirements, but I don't think it will serve the detainees there well. And that people who— often too many people in Rikers, and hopefully we're going to speed up our case processing and get people in and out of our pre-trial detention systems more

quickly— but with so many people in there for one year, two year, three years, not having real access to outdoor space is just profoundly harmful to someone's mental health. So there is a roof space.
